Content: Units and conversions are the strict rules of measurement that allow mathematical models to span different types of quantities. A `ultext(Unit)` is a standardized quantity used to express a physical measurement – such as a foot, a liter, a dollar, or a second. Numbers without units have no meaning in real-world situations. Telling someone a race is “`26`” is useless without clarifying whether we mean `text(26 miles)` or `text(26 meters)`. In fields like aerospace engineering, medicine, and international trade, units allow us to identify precise solutions with measurement constraints. In fact, NASA once lost a `text($125 million)` Mars orbiter because one engineering team used metric units while another used imperial units.

On the SAT exam, mastering units and conversions is an essential skill in the Problem Solving and Data Analysis category. Often times, SAT problem don't include units that perfectly align with one another from start to finish. Instead, we might come across a word problem where the rate is in gallons per hour but the answer choices are in cups per minute. Simply crunching the numbers without paying close attention to the units may lead us to choose an answer choice that would make sense if all the units were the same. Learning to handle units as algebraic variables that can be multiplied, divided, and canceled out lets us navigate complex multi-step word problems with absolute certainty.

Dismantling these problems requires an understanding of the relationship between unit rates and conversion factors. A `ultext(Unit Rate)` is a comparison of two quantities with different units where the second quantity is reduced to exactly one unit. Everyday examples include driving at a rate of `60` miles per (`1`) hour or buying apples for `$3` per (`1`) pound. On the SAT exam, a unit rate acts as a bridge that tells us exactly how many times greater one quantity is than a single unit of another quantity.

When it's necessary to change measurements to a different scale, we can perform a `ultext(Unit Conversion)` using conversion factors. A `ultext(Conversion Factor)` is a fraction or ratio that expresses equivalence between two quantities with different units. Because the two parts of the ratio represent the exact same physical quantity in the real-world – such as `text(12 inches)/text(1 foot)` or `text(60 minutes)/text(1 hour)` – the value of a conversion factor with units included is equal to `1`. Multiplying an expression by a conversion factor changes its appearance and units of measurement , but does not actually alter its physical value.

The best strategy for executing unit conversions is a process called dimensional analysis (or the factor-label method). `ultext(Dimensional Analysis)` involves setting up conversion factor fractions so that the units we want to get rid of cancel out diagonally, leaving only the desired units in the solution. For example, if asked to convert `text(180 inches)` into feet, we can multiply the original value by a conversion factor that places inches in the denominator. This would look like `text(180 inches)*(text(1 foot)/text(12 inches))=180/12text( feet)=text(15 feet)`. Because inches appear on the top of the first term and the bottom of the second term, they cancel out entirely, leaving feet as the lone unit that remains. Many SAT problems will bury unit changes within dense word problems, so it's important to carefully recognize different units and understand how one quantity compares to another.
